target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove the main scheduling barrier to voting.
objection: A federal holiday would not reliably remove the scheduling barrier because federal law does not require private employers to close or provide paid time off, so many low-wage workers in retail, food service, and similar jobs would still have to work or take unpaid time off to vote.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday would not meaningfully change people’s schedules and would still leave low-income workers disadvantaged.
objection: A federal holiday does change the practical schedule people are operating under: schools close, many businesses reduce staffing or shut down, and election officials can use holiday-available workers to make polling places more usable, so the holiday can create real daytime voting availability even without legally forcing every employer to close.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday-driven schedule changes will create broad daytime voting access.
objection: Even if some businesses adjust, many essential low-wage workplaces stay open on federal holidays, so the workers most constrained by work schedules may still need unpaid time off or to vote around shifts; therefore the holiday’s effect is uneven and does not eliminate the time constraint for those voters.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday still leaves the core scheduling barrier intact because employers may not give time off.
objection: The holiday can reduce scheduling barriers even without universal employer closure because it changes the actual timing structure of the day, lets election officials staff polling places with holiday-available workers, and gives voters more usable hours before or after shifts rather than depending entirely on employer permission.

target: AG1’s claim that polling-place staffing and holiday timing are enough to decouple voting from employer-provided time off.
objection: The real constraint is whether workers are actually free during voting hours to travel, wait, and return; many hourly jobs still operate on holidays, so access still depends on employers allowing time away or on workers losing wages, which means the holiday does not decouple voting from employer discretion.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday timing cannot meaningfully reduce the scheduling barrier because employers may still keep people working.
objection: International practice shows that holiday or weekend elections can meaningfully improve access: 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays, which supports the idea that shifting election day can reduce scheduling barriers rather than just moving them around.

target: AG1’s reliance on OECD holiday/weekend elections as proof that a U.S. federal holiday would have the same effect.
objection: The OECD comparison does not prove the U.S. would get the same turnout/access effect because the U.S. system still lets private employers keep workers on the job, so the burden can simply shift from “polling hours vs. workdays” to “polling hours vs. whether your employer gives time off,” leaving the constraint largely intact for low-income workers.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday only shifts burdens and does not meaningfully create usable time for many voters.
objection: A federal holiday also removes major school and childcare conflicts for parents and caretakers, since schools close and normal school-based obligations disappear, which can free up daytime hours and reduce dependence on employer approval or wage loss.

target: AG1’s claim that school closures would meaningfully free up low-income parents to vote.
objection: Many low-income parents rely on daycare, Head Start, paid sitters, or informal caregivers that do not close just because schools do, so school closure alone does not reliably create true voting availability and may still leave parents needing unpaid time off or extra childcare logistics.

target: AG2’s claim that school closures won’t reliably help because childcare often does not follow the school calendar.
objection: In many households, childcare is tied to the school calendar through school-based or school-linked programs, so closing schools does change parents’ daytime responsibilities and can create a workable window for voting for a substantial share of families.

target: AG1’s claim that school/childcare changes are enough to make a holiday a reliable turnout reform.
objection: Even if schools close and some childcare changes, research indicates an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with other reforms; easing one schedule constraint does not reliably solve the core problem that many low-wage workers still need paid time or wage protection to vote.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday only changes a minor school routine and leaves the core barrier untouched.
objection: The holiday changes the broader weekday coordination system—work hours, school obligations, and childcare logistics—so it can create real daytime availability and reduce the need to choose between voting and staying at work, making access meaningfully better without requiring universal paid leave.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday-induced schedule changes make voting practically feasible for many parents and workers.
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to close or give paid time, and many hourly jobs still run on holidays, so workers may still need unpaid time off or lose wages; substitute childcare may also remain necessary, so the core constraint for low-income workers persists.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday mainly rearranges logistics without improving the core constraint.
objection: The holiday changes more than one small detail: it shifts school and childcare routines, alters weekday work coordination, and lets election administration match polling logistics to newly workable daytime windows, so it can meaningfully expand access for many voters.

target: AG1’s claim that the school/childcare effect reliably expands workable voting time.
objection: Even when schools close, many parents still face childcare and work constraints because private workplaces stay open and childcare arrangements may not follow public-school calendars, so the holiday does not reliably create new voting availability and can still leave wage loss or substitute-care burdens in place.

target: AG2’s claim that persistent workplace and childcare constraints prevent the holiday from being broadly effective.
objection: The holiday addresses the real coordination problem by changing both the weekday school/childcare structure and many workplace routines, while election officials can adapt polling schedules to the holiday; that makes the holiday a plausible broad access reform rather than an ineffective symbolic gesture.
